newsitem.title: USA: Clinton focuses on jokes, card games, basketball.
newsitem.headline: Clinton focuses on jokes, card games, basketball.

text.p: From the moment President Bill Clinton heard a "very loud pop" in the leg he once injured skiing he knew he was in trouble, but although he was in pain he was also in good spirits, aides said.

Clinton attempted to cover his pain and frustration at tearing a tendon in the early hours of Friday, waving to bystanders, cracking jokes, playing cards and anticipating watching the U.S. college basketball tournament.

"He's disappointed to be missing golf in the spring and summer," senior White House aide Bruce Lindsey told reporters travelling on Air Force One. "... (But) if you have to be laid up, you might as well do it during March Madness," he added in a reference to the televised NCAA basketball tournament.

Clinton tore a quadriceps tendon in his right thigh around 1:20 a.m. EST (0620 GMT) when he twisted his leg on some steps at the south Florida estate of Australian golf legend Greg Norman, White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn said.
"He remembers his right leg, his right knee buckling out. He heard a very loud pop and felt some pain in his right leg," Glynn said.

The injury will require surgery as well as weeks in a splint and on crutches, followed by rehabilitation therapy. It was the same leg that Clinton injured while skiing about 17 years ago. He did not have surgery at the time.
"He's in good shape," said Lindsey, who played the card game Hearts with Clinton at St. Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach, Florida. "He was in a good mood."
Clinton had been looking forward to a big weekend of golf in Florida and was trying to remain upbeat.

"I saw Greg Norman this morning. I told him my handicap is going up by the minute," Clinton joked in a telephone conference call from Air Force One to schoolchildren he was supposed to have visited in Jupiter, Florida on Friday.

Witnesses at the hospital said Clinton waved to them and smiled as he was wheeled into the hospital emergency room on a stretcher. Glynn said the president was well enough to feel "bored" during a long session of magnetic resonance imaging.

Clinton left the hospital by wheelchair, heading for home more than a day early. It took several people to half-carry him from a station wagon in his motorcade onto a make-shift wheelchair, which was carried up a short staircase into the presidential aircraft. His right leg was extended and braced.

He managed a smile for reporters and a thumbs-up when asked how he felt before he was lifted onto the plane. Asked whether he would proceed with a planned summit meeting in Helsinki, Finland, next week with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, Clinton replied: "It'll go on, you bet."
